section_1.title: Introduction: The Goal of Mathematical Clarity
section_1.content: Define an 'effective' explanation as one that bridges the gap between the teacher's internal logic and the student's cognitive map. Emphasize that clarity is not just about correctness, but about psychological accessibility.
section_1.example: Comparing an abstract formula to a map: A good explanation provides a legend (context) and a clear path (logic), not just the destination.

section_2.title: Criterion 1: Scaffolding and Prerequisite Alignment
section_2.content: Before introducing a complex concept, activate prior knowledge. Use visual 'layering'—start with a solid base (familiar knowledge) before building the new concept on top.
section_2.example: Before explaining the 'Chain Rule' in Calculus, show a quick animation of nested gears (a small gear rotating a larger one) to visualize function composition.

section_3.title: Criterion 2: The Power of Multi-Representational Fluency
section_3.content: An effective explanation must move between verbal, algebraic, and graphical representations. Visual-spatial reasoning reduces the cognitive load of abstract symbolic manipulation.
section_3.example: Explaining the Pythagorean theorem ($a² + b² = c²$) using an animation of water flowing between squares built on the sides of a triangle, transitioning from geometry to algebra.

section_4.title: Criterion 3: Precision vs. Intuition (The 'Just-in-Time' Rule)
section_4.content: Balance rigor with intuition. Introduce high-level formalism only after the intuitive 'hook' is established. Use characters or scenarios to anchor abstract principles.
section_4.example: Teaching 'Probability' by animating a robot choosing paths in a labyrinth. The robot counts total exits (the sample space) before calculating the odds of reaching a specific prize.

section_5.title: Conclusion: Reflection and Self-Check
section_5.content: Summarize the three pillars: (1) Scaffolding, (2) Multi-representation, and (3) Intuitive grounding. Emphasize that the final test of an explanation is whether the listener can 're-teach' it back to you.
section_5.example: Final slide: A checklist graphic titled 'The Clarity Compass' that students can use to audit their future presentations.

class TeachingScene(Scene):

        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=20, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]

        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])

        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]

        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom

        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
